title: Prayer as rhythm
hook: Muslim daily prayer gives the whole day five fixed moments to come back to

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mevlevi: Rumi's order, turning in the sema as an act of remembrance. Your line was not a performance. Did one thing you did change when you stopped doing it for an audience? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

It's still dark. A call to prayer drifts from a minaret, or a phone chimes softly on a nightstand. Someone gets up, washes face, hands and arms, wipes the head, washes the feet, turns toward Mecca, and stands. A few minutes later, the day begins. Just after noon, in an office or a stockroom, it happens again. In the afternoon, again. Just after sunset. And once more at night. Between those moments are meetings and school runs, dishes and traffic. The prayer doesn't replace any of that. It stitches it together. Today's word is less a word than a shape: prayer as rhythm.
screen: `STILL DARK. A CALL, A CHIME.` → `WASH, TURN, STAND.` → `AGAIN AT NOON. AGAIN AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word for this prayer is salah. In one place the Qur'an ties it to the clock: prayer, it says, is prescribed for believers at set times. The number comes from the hadith. In a long account in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is given fifty prayers a day on the Night Journey. On the advice of Moses he goes back, again and again, to ask for fewer, until they stand at five. Muslims name them by their hour: fajr at dawn, dhuhr after midday, asr in the afternoon, maghrib after sunset, isha at night. The times follow the sun, so they drift through the year. The schedule isn't set by a boss or a calendar. It's set by the sky. Another hadith gives the rhythm a picture. The Prophet asks his companions: if a river ran past your door, and you bathed in it five times a day, would any dirt be left on you? None, they say. That, he tells them, is what the five prayers are like: through them God washes away wrongs. Inside each prayer there is a rhythm too. Standing, reciting, bowing, going down with the forehead to the ground, sitting, and up again. In every prayer the opening chapter of the Qur'an is recited, which begins, in Pickthall's English: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." A rule tells you what to do. A rhythm tells you when to come back. Whatever happened at three o'clock, the afternoon prayer is waiting at the same door, and the same words are waiting inside it.
screen: `SALAH, AT SET TIMES.` · `FIFTY, BROUGHT DOWN TO FIVE.` · `A RIVER PAST YOUR DOOR.` · `STAND, BOW, BOW DOWN, SIT.` · then, large: `PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel your day's rhythm. This isn't salah, and it isn't meant to stand in for it. It's a way to notice the shape of your own day. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Walk through the day in your mind: waking. The middle of the day. The afternoon. The light going at sunset. The last minutes before sleep. At each one, ask: what usually happens here? Where do I already pause, and where do I rush straight through? If you pray, notice where a prayer already lives, or could. The bell holds the time.
Prayer as rhythm. Salah, the Muslim daily prayer, kept at five moments that move with the sun, giving the whole day places to return to. Today's word.
Your line: a rhythm. Today, pick one of those moments, maybe sunset, and when it comes, stop for one full breath before you carry on. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Muslims pray salah five times a day at times set by the sun, from dawn to night, after washing and facing toward Mecca; each prayer moves through standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, and the opening chapter of the Qur'an is recited in every one.
